findings.documented: the API key is appended as a query parameter, GET /v1/listings?api_key=...
findings.actual: the key must be sent in an X-API-Key request header; sending it as a query parameter returns 401 and the error body says so
findings.how_found: first authenticated call of the session failed; read the 401 body instead of assuming the reference was right
findings.impact: nothing works until this is fixed, so it blocks every other endpoint

findings.documented: the body is email and password; the key is not mentioned for this endpoint
findings.actual: login also requires the X-API-Key header, and returns 401 without it
findings.how_found: login failed with the documented body until the key header was added
findings.impact: a client that only sends credentials cannot obtain a token

findings.documented: the response field holding the token is called `token`
findings.actual: the field is `access_token`; there is also `refresh_token` and `refresh_url`
findings.how_found: compared the documented response shape against the keys actually returned
findings.impact: reading `token` yields undefined, and the session silently never authenticates

findings.documented: expires_in is 86400, and a single login is enough for one working session
findings.actual: expires_in is 900, so the access token lasts fifteen minutes
findings.how_found: read expires_in from the login response and decoded the token payload
findings.impact: a long crawl or a browsing session dies partway through unless it re-authenticates

findings.documented: tokens last 24 hours and there is no refresh flow
findings.actual: POST /auth/refresh exists and takes {"refresh_token": ...}; the login response even advertises it in refresh_url
findings.how_found: probed the path after the 900 second TTL made a refresh mechanism likely
findings.impact: without it the app cannot stay usable, and the crawl truncates on expiry

findings.documented: collections take `page`, 1-indexed, and `limit`
findings.actual: `page` is accepted and silently ignored; the window is moved by `offset`
findings.how_found: requested limit=5&page=2 and compared the returned ids against page 1 - identical
findings.impact: paging by `page` re-reads the first window forever, so any count derived that way is wrong and nothing warns you

findings.documented: limit may be up to 200
findings.actual: limit is silently clamped to 50; the envelope reports limit=50 for any larger request, with no error
findings.how_found: asked for 100, 200, 500 and 1000 and read back the limit the envelope reported
findings.impact: a client trusting the documented maximum makes four times fewer requests than it needs and stops early

findings.documented: responses are shaped {total, page, page_size, results}
findings.actual: responses are {limit, offset, count, total, has_more, results}
findings.how_found: read the raw envelope on the first call rather than the documented example
findings.impact: page_size and page do not exist, so a client reading them gets undefined

findings.documented: total is the exact number of records matching your filters; to fetch every record, read total, divide by your limit, and request that many pages
findings.actual: total reports 3749 while 4100 records are retrievable; the shortfall is about 8.6% and it holds under filters too (property_type=plot reports 126 against 138 served). Following the documented procedure loses 351 listings
findings.how_found: paged to exhaustion with limit=50, then again with limit=25, then a third time ordered by price; all three traversals returned the same 4100 distinct ids
findings.impact: every count in an analysis built on total is short by 8.6%, including the record count, the live count and the seven-day count

findings.documented: a single listing is served from /v1/listing/{listing_id}
findings.actual: 404; the path that works is /v1/listings/{listing_id}
findings.how_found: called both spellings with an id taken from the collection
findings.impact: a detail page built on the documented path 404s for every listing

findings.documented: up to ten comparable listings, same locality, same bedroom count, price within 15%
findings.how_found: called it with a known-good listing id
findings.impact: the documented 'you may also like' strip cannot be built from this endpoint

findings.documented: a logged-in user can save listings via GET, POST and DELETE /v1/favourites
findings.actual: 404 on all three methods, with both the British and American spellings
findings.how_found: called each method with a valid token and a valid listing id
findings.impact: saved listings has no server side at all, so per-user persistence has to be built client side

findings.documented: pre-computed aggregates for the city: total_listings, median_price, median_price_per_sqft, by_locality, by_bhk
findings.how_found: called it while building the insights screen
findings.impact: every figure on an analytics screen has to be computed from the listing records instead

findings.documented: not in the reference
findings.actual: exists and returns {city, count, results} - the authoritative list of locality spellings for the city
findings.how_found: probed plausible paths after /v1/analytics/summary turned out to be absent
findings.impact: it is the only reliable source for the locality filter, since that filter is an exact match

findings.documented: not in the reference
findings.actual: exists unauthenticated and returns a service descriptor that names /health, /register and /llms.txt
findings.how_found: opened the base URL in a browser before writing any client code
findings.impact: it advertises paths the reference never mentions

findings.documented: not in the reference
findings.actual: exists unauthenticated, 3001 bytes, advertised by GET / as for_agents
findings.how_found: followed the for_agents pointer from the service root
findings.impact: it publishes per-city figures for four of the assignment's questions, and they disagree with the API: it claims 3916 listing records for this city against 4100 retrievable

findings.documented: project_id filters the collection - the reference states that total_listings always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns
findings.actual: project_id is accepted and ignored; the response is byte-identical to the unfiltered window
findings.how_found: requested a real project_id and compared the returned id list against the unfiltered baseline
findings.impact: a per-project listing count cannot be obtained from the API and has to be derived from a full crawl

findings.documented: sort_by accepts price, carpet_area, posted_at and bedroom
findings.actual: price and bedroom sort correctly; carpet_area and posted_at change the order but the result is not sorted by those fields
findings.how_found: requested each field ascending and descending and checked the returned values for monotonicity
findings.impact: a client offering 'newest first' or 'largest first' shows an order that looks deliberate and is not

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees
findings.actual: they are in Indian display units, where the unit depends on the magnitude: a value below 10 is crores and a value of 10 or more is lakhs. Measured as listings_max/price_max, which splits cleanly into 431 projects at about 1e7 and 27 at about 1.5e5, and price_min splits the same way at 384 and 76 - matching the digit counts exactly
findings.how_found: the raw values made price_min exceed price_max for 357 of 460 projects, which is impossible for a minimum and a maximum, so the multiplier was measured against each project's own listing prices rather than assumed
findings.impact: taken literally the costliest project is wrong by a factor of 26, and every project price shown to a user is wrong by 100x one way or the other

findings.documented: area is square feet, integer, everywhere in the API
findings.actual: 333 records state carpet_area and super_built_up_area in square metres. The two groups do not overlap: the square-metre values run 34 to 197 and the square-foot values start at 206, and super/carpet stays near 1.34 in both, so these are small units rather than small flats
findings.how_found: a duplicate cluster held four records near 1261 sqft and one at 113; 113 x 10.7639 is 1216
findings.impact: rupees per square foot comes out 63.7% too high if these are left alone, and the affected records never match their own duplicates on area

findings.documented: deposit is the security deposit in rupees
findings.actual: 301 records give deposit as a number of months instead. Their values run 2 to 10, and multiplying by that record's rent lands them on the same distribution as the rupee records, whose deposit is a median 6 months of rent
findings.how_found: the digit histogram was bimodal - about 300 records in the single and double digits against 1249 in the five and six digit range
findings.impact: a deposit of 6 is shown to a user as six rupees

findings.documented: timestamps are ISO 8601, UTC, with a Z suffix, everywhere in the API
findings.actual: posted_at carries no timezone marker at all on any of the 4100 records, and the clock is IST: /health reports timezone Asia/Kolkata and a reference_date with a +05:30 offset
findings.how_found: classified every posted_at string by format; all 4100 were naive ISO
findings.impact: reading them as UTC shifts the seven-day window by five and a half hours and changes the count from 122 to 106

findings.documented: one timestamp convention for the whole API
findings.actual: listings use naive ISO with no offset while rentals use a Z suffix - two formats in the same API, and neither collection matches the other
findings.how_found: the same format classifier run over both collections
findings.impact: a single parser written against either collection mis-reads the other

findings.documented: returns active sale listings only; inactive, expired and withdrawn listings are excluded server side, so anything returned is safe to show a user
findings.actual: 867 of 4100 retrievable records have is_live false, and is_live is not in the documented listing object at all
findings.how_found: counted is_live across the full crawl after noticing the reference never mentions the field
findings.impact: a client trusting the documentation shows withdrawn listings to users

findings.documented: every listing_id is globally unique, and each listing corresponds to exactly one physical property
findings.actual: the first half is true - 4100 ids, 4100 distinct. The second is not: the same property is syndicated across portals under different ids, and 983 records are a second or later copy of a property already present, leaving 3117 distinct properties
findings.how_found: matched on geometry rather than text, because copies jitter the coordinates and re-type the building name - they agree on apartment_name only 48% of the time. Within 100 m, same bedroom, carpet within 2%, same floor and facing, the cluster count is flat from 100 m through 300 m
findings.impact: any count, average or listing page treats one flat as five, and 79% of these pairs cross portals so a user sees the same property repeatedly

findings.documented: the listing object describes a real property; description is the seller's own text and posted_by_contact is a verified contact number
findings.actual: 63 records describe something that cannot exist, in seven disjoint groups of exactly nine: non-positive price, price under a lakh, carpet area larger than super built up area, floor above total_floors, coordinates outside the city, posted_at after the reference moment, and no bedroom and no bathroom on a non-plot property
findings.how_found: ran impossibility predicates over the full crawl. The count of nine recurring across unrelated defects is what made the set identifiable - and it is also what ruled out the 133 records a naive area check flags, which are the square-metre records rather than corrupt ones
findings.impact: they poison any mean that divides by price or area, which is why question 6 excludes them

findings.documented: posted_by_contact is the seller's verified contact number, and is_verified means the operations team has checked the listing
findings.actual: 110 listings across 7 phone numbers are not genuine. Each of those numbers has a fully verified portfolio while the market runs at 60% verified, every one of its listings is priced below its locality and bedroom median with none above 0.79 of it, and each number posts under three to six different seller names
findings.how_found: volume alone separates nothing - the five largest portfolios in the city are ordinary agents at 38% to 73% verified and market prices. The three signals together leave a clean gap: the next contact down is 29% verified with one name and prices above the median
findings.impact: is_verified is worse than useless here, since being fully verified is the signal of the fake set. Contact details shown to users route enquiries to these numbers

findings.documented: total_listings is the number of listings currently available in the project, recomputed whenever a listing is added or withdrawn, so it always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns
findings.actual: it disagrees for 119 of 460 projects when counted against the live listings actually served
findings.how_found: counted live listings per project_id from the full crawl, since the project_id filter is ignored. Of the readings tried, currently-available - is_live true - leaves 341 projects exactly correct with no bias in the error; counting all records instead leaves only 124 correct, which describes a wrong rule rather than a broken field
findings.impact: a project page showing this number is wrong about a quarter of the time
